note: Base-rate reference data for relationship/marriage outcomes. Figures are approximate, drawn from widely-cited public research (US CDC/NCHS marriage-divorce data, longitudinal relationship studies, Pew, and academic dissolution research). Treat as planning base rates, not precise truths. Each factor lists directional effect on the odds a relationship endures. The reasoning model uses these as grounding, not as a lookup table.
sources_general: Longitudinal relationship-dissolution research (e.g., Gottman body of work; Stanford How Couples Meet studies)

factors.note: Marrying very young is one of the strongest predictors of divorce.
Later marriage correlates with greater stability, up to a point.
Wider age gaps correlate with higher dissolution rates.
Higher education correlates with marital stability.
Remarriages dissolve at higher rates than first marriages.
Historically associated with slightly higher divorce risk; effect is debated and shrinking.
Financial compatibility and low money-conflict predict stability.
Contempt and stonewalling are among the strongest predictors of breakup (Gottman).
Long distance raises dissolution risk modestly; many survive it.
Couples embedded in shared networks tend to last longer.

mirror_stats: About 43% of first marriages in the US end in divorce — meaning most, but not all, endure.
Roughly 60% of second marriages end in divorce, a higher rate than firsts.
The single strongest predictor of a breakup isn't conflict — it's contempt.
Couples who marry after 25 divorce at markedly lower rates than those who marry before 20.
Around half of dating relationships don't survive their first year — the ones that do have already beaten the odds.
